text: Etty left school at 12 and went to work as a printer's apprentice in Hull. Seven years later he moved to London and joined the Royal Academy Schools, where he studied under Thomas Lawrence. His painting Cleopatra's Arrival in Cilicia, shown in 1821, was full of nudes, and it brought him success. He was elected a Royal Academician in 1828, though some people called his nudes indecent. He never married. He retired to York in 1848 and died the following year, shortly after a big exhibition of his work.

Landseer showed his work at the Royal Academy at 13, long before he was old enough to join it. His father was an engraver, and the painter Benjamin Robert Haydon urged him to dissect animals so he could learn how muscles and bones fit together. He became an Academician in 1831 and was knighted in 1850. Queen Victoria gave him many commissions, starting with her pets and moving on to portraits of her babies. He declined the presidency of the Royal Academy. Near the end of his life his family had him declared insane.

Largillière grew up in Antwerp, where his family moved when he was about three. After leaving his first teacher he worked for Peter Lely at Windsor for four years. Charles II wanted to keep him as a court painter, but the Rye House Plot frightened him and he left for Paris. In 1686 he painted a portrait of Charles Le Brun to get into the Académie royale. Le Brun liked it and let him in. James II later offered him the post of keeper of the royal collections, but he said no.

Short started out as a civil engineer and worked on the Thames pollution inquiry before he turned to art. He joined the South Kensington School of Art in 1883. His first successes were etchings and mezzotints after Turner's Liber Studiorum, and John Ruskin gave him praise and advice along the way. Whistler became his friend. Short led the Royal Society of Painter Etchers and Engravers from 1910 to 1938. Low shores and river estuaries held his attention for his whole working life, and he returned to them again and again in his prints.

Liebenwein was keener on animals than on lessons, and he left the Vienna Academy in 1891. He served in a dragoon regiment, tried a school for historical painting and then moved on to Karlsruhe. In Munich he took classes with Heinrich von Zügel, who taught animal painting. From 1897 he worked as an independent painter. On a visit to Burghausen with a friend, he saw the medieval castle. It impressed them both. He later became vice president of the Vienna Secession and showed with the group many times.

Cranach learned to draw from his father in Kronach, and the family name Maler simply meant painter. In 1504 he joined the court of Frederick the Wise at Wittenberg, and he served the Electors of Saxony for the rest of his life. He became a close friend of Martin Luther, and eleven portraits of the reformer by him survive. His workshop was big, so many pictures exist in several versions. His son Lucas Cranach the Younger kept making versions of them for decades after his death. Nudes from myth and the Bible stayed part of his work throughout his career.

Enea Vico lost his mother at his birth and his father when he was two, and he grew up in a noble family from Parma. He began working young in Parma and Rome, then moved on to Florence and Venice. He engraved grotesques based on antique paintings and made prints for Cosimo I de' Medici. In 1550 he published a book called Donne Auguste while staying at the court in Augsburg. In 1563 he joined the court of Alfonso II d'Este at Ferrara, and he made about five hundred engravings in all. He was also a known numismatist.

Tanner decided to become a painter at about 13, after he watched a landscape artist at work in Fairmount Park. His middle name Ossawa recalled the fighting at Osawatomie between pro and anti slavery groups. In 1879 he enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in Philadelphia, and he was the only black student there. Thomas Eakins taught him, and Tanner became one of his favorite students. Eakins painted his portrait two decades after Tanner left. In 1891 Tanner moved to Paris to study at the Académie Julian.

Lépine painted the Seine in all its moods for the rest of his life. He grew up in Caen and met Corot in Normandy in 1859, then became his student the following year. He joined the First Impressionist Exhibition at Nadar's in 1874, though people don't usually count him as an Impressionist. His paintings are calm and mostly small. A gold medal at the Exposition Universelle of 1889 went to his Pont de l'Estacade. He died suddenly in Paris in 1892.

Bernard Picart taught Van der Schley, and he copied his master's style for years afterwards. He mostly engraved portraits and made illustrations, among them pictures for Marivaux's novel La Vie de Marianne, which came out in The Hague over several years. In 1740 he engraved the frontispieces for a 15 volume edition of the works of Brantôme. Most plates in the Hague edition of Prévost's Histoire générale des voyages carry his signature. He worked with Prosper Marchand, who owned many of his prints. He died in Amsterdam in 1779.

Sichem came from a Roman Catholic family of Dutch engravers and publishers that kept the trade going for four generations. He was born in Basel, where his father had moved in 1570 to work as a printmaker. The family went to Amsterdam in 1599. Most of his work was reproductive, which means he cut prints after pictures and prints by others, such as Goltzius, Holbein and Heemskerck. He also made a series of woodcuts of famous people after prints by his father. In 1646 he published a collection of his own work.

Moulijn grew up in Rotterdam as the son of a manufacturer and merchant, and he studied at the academies in Rotterdam and Amsterdam. At the Amsterdam academy he met Richard Roland Holst and Isaac Israëls. After his studies ended in 1887 he wandered between Drenthe, Rotterdam, The Hague and Renkum. The Symbolism of Maurice Maeterlinck strongly shaped his early work. Around 1893 he found his own style. A one man show at S. Bing's gallery in Paris in 1896 was his first big success.

Franco, nicknamed il Semolei, came to Rome from Venice in his twenties. He painted an allegory of the Battle of Montemurlo, which now hangs in the Pitti Palace, and a fresco of the Arrest of John the Baptist in 1541. His style leaned heavily on Michelangelo, but his drawings and etchings have more energy and fresh ideas. Back in Venice he helped paint the ceiling of the Biblioteca Marciana. He also painted panels for the Grimani chapel in San Francesco della Vigna. His son Giacomo became an etcher and publisher.

Carrière decided to become an artist in 1868, when he saw the paintings of Rubens in the Louvre while working as a lithographer. He studied under Alexandre Cabanel, but the Franco Prussian War broke into his studies and he was taken prisoner. His brother found him part time work at the Sèvres porcelain factory, and there he met Auguste Rodin. They stayed close friends. A Salon painting of his earned an honourable mention in 1884, and the critic Roger Marx began to back him. His pictures are done in a nearly one colour brown palette.

Müller saw the Bristol riots of 1831 and recorded some of the scenes in raw, quick sketches. He was born in Bristol, the son of a Prussian museum curator, and studied under James Baker Pyne. In 1838 he set out for Athens, Alexandria and Cairo, then went up the Nile to Luxor to draw the ruins. His scenes of Egyptian streets and markets sold well. Later he travelled to Lycia at his own expense, with his pupil Harry Johnson, and spent three months sketching there. He died in Bristol in 1845, and fakes of his work soon appeared.

Schiavone means the Slav, a nickname for Andrea Meldolla, who was born in Zara in Dalmatia, where his father was a garrison commander, and both of his parents came from Romagna. He taught himself to etch, working at first from drawings by Parmigianino. By 1540 he was established enough in Venice that Vasari commissioned a large battle picture from him. He later influenced Titian, Tintoretto and Jacopo Bassano. Few of his paintings are documented. Vasari says he mostly worked for private clients.

Pool was born and died in Amsterdam. He worked with Gerard de Lairesse on the engravings for his Groot schilderboeck, and with the painter Barend Graat on prints after ivory sculptures by Francis van Bossuit. In 1708 he married Graat's daughter and moved to the Leidsegracht. Most of his prints copy the work of other artists. He also made topographical views and pictures of the Bentvueghels.

Ismael Mengs, a Danish born painter, raised his son Anton in Dresden and then in Rome from 1741, where he copied Raphael in miniature for the Elector of Saxony. Eight years later the son became first painter to the Elector. In Rome he made a full size copy of Raphael's School of Athens for the Duke of Northumberland. He went to Madrid at the call of Charles III and painted a banqueting hall ceiling in the Royal Palace. Mengs died in Rome in 1779. He left twenty children.
